turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Not much, I guess. Just the usual stuff. I've been working on a project that I'm really interested in, and I've been putting in a lot of hours on it. I've also been dealing with some issues at home with my family, but that's just normal stuff, right?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like you've got a lot on your plate, between your project and some family issues. That can be really overwhelming. Just because family issues might be common, doesn't mean they're not affecting you. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been going on at home? What kind of issues have you been dealing with, and how have you been feeling about them?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I...don't know. It's just...my mom's been getting on my case about stuff, and it's hard to explain. I mean, I like things a certain way, and she doesn't understand that. She just keeps saying I'm being "difficult" or "picky," but it's not that. It's just that some things are important to me, you know? Like, I like to eat the same breakfast every day, and she keeps trying to get me to eat something different. It's just...it's hard to deal with her not getting it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It can be really frustrating when someone doesn't understand or respect our needs and preferences. It sounds like you're feeling a bit misunderstood and maybe even a little criticized by your mom. That can be a really tough spot to be in, especially when it's someone close to you who's not getting it. It's like, you're trying to explain something that feels really important to you, and she's just not hearing you.

Can you tell me more about what it's like for you when your mom tries to get you to eat something different for breakfast? How does that make you feel, and what's going through your mind in those moments?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It makes me feel...anxious, I guess. Like, I start thinking about all the things that could go wrong if I eat something different. Will I get a stomachache? Will I feel weird? It's hard to explain, but it's like my whole mind is racing with all these worst-case scenarios. And then my mom just gets mad at me because I'm being "picky" again, like it's my fault or something. It's really frustrating. Can you be more specific about what you mean by "how does that make you feel"? Like, do you want me to rate my feelings on a scale or something?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
No, no scales or ratings needed. I just want to understand what's going on for you in those moments. When I ask "how does that make you feel," I'm trying to get a sense of what's happening emotionally for you. It sounds like you're experiencing some anxiety, like your mind is racing with worries about what might happen if you eat something different. That can be a really uncomfortable and overwhelming feeling.

I'm also picking up on some feelings of frustration and maybe even a bit of hurt, like you feel your mom isn't understanding or validating your needs. It's like you're trying to communicate something important to her, and she's not hearing you. Does that sound about right?

Also, I want to gently explore this a bit further. You mentioned that your mind starts racing with worst-case scenarios when your mom suggests eating something different. Have you noticed if this kind of thinking happens in other areas of your life, or is it mostly related to food and your mom's suggestions?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think that's kind of right. I feel anxious and frustrated, and it's hard to explain to my mom because she just doesn't get it. And yeah, it's not just about food, I guess. It's just that when things are different, it's hard for me to...not think about all the things that could go wrong. Like, I was trying to explain this to my friend the other day, and I was thinking about what if the bus is late, and what if I miss my stop, and what if it rains...and my friend just laughed and said "oh, you're just being paranoid." But it's not that I'm being paranoid, it's just that I'm thinking about all the possibilities. Does that make sense?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you have a very active and vigilant mind, always thinking about potential outcomes and possibilities. That can be both a strength and a challenge, I imagine. On the one hand, it's great that you're able to think critically and anticipate potential problems. On the other hand, it can be overwhelming and anxiety-provoking when your mind is constantly racing with "what-ifs."

It's interesting that your friend responded by saying you're being paranoid. I can see how that might be frustrating, because it sounds like you're not just being paranoid, but rather, you're trying to prepare for potential outcomes. It's like you're trying to be proactive and in control, but that's being misunderstood by others.

I want to acknowledge that it takes a lot of courage to share this with me, and I'm here to listen and try to understand. It sounds like you might be experiencing some anxiety that goes beyond just the situation with your mom and food. Would you be open to exploring this further, and seeing if there are any patterns or themes that might be contributing to your anxiety?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I don't know...I just feel like people never get it. They always think I'm being weird or paranoid, but I'm just trying to think ahead and be prepared. It's not that I don't like surprises or anything, it's just that...safety is important to me, I guess. I like to know what's going to happen and how to deal with it. But it's hard to explain that to people who don't understand.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're feeling a bit isolated in your experiences and concerns. Like, you're trying to communicate something important to others, but they're not getting it, and that can be really frustrating and lonely.

I want to acknowledge that it's totally reasonable to prioritize safety and preparation. It's a fundamental human need to feel secure and in control, and it sounds like that's really important to you. It's not about being "weird" or "paranoid," but rather, it's about taking care of yourself and being proactive.

I'm here to listen and try to understand, and I want you to know that I'm not judging you. I'm trying to get a sense of what's going on for you, and how I can support you. It's okay to have different needs and concerns than others, and it's okay to prioritize your own safety and well-being.

If you're willing, I'd like to explore this idea of safety and preparation further. What does safety mean to you, and how do you typically try to achieve it in your daily life? Are there any specific situations or experiences that make you feel particularly anxious or uncertain?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Safety means being in control and knowing what's going to happen. It means having a plan and being prepared for anything. For me, it's about following routines and sticking to what I know. If I know what's going to happen, I feel safer. But if things change or get unpredictable, it's really hard for me. I get anxious and feel overwhelmed. I try to stay in my comfort zone, where I feel like I can control things.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like having a sense of control and predictability is really crucial for you, and that's what helps you feel safe. And when things get unpredictable or outside of your control, that's when you start to feel anxious and overwhelmed.

It's like you have a sense of a "comfort zone" that you try to stay within, where you feel like you can manage things and anticipate what's going to happen. And when you're outside of that zone, it's like you're in uncharted territory, and that can be really scary.

I want to acknowledge that it takes a lot of courage to admit when you're feeling overwhelmed or anxious. It's not always easy to talk about, especially if you feel like others might not understand.

I'm here to support you, and I want to help you explore ways to manage your anxiety and feel more in control. One thing that might be helpful is to identify some specific coping strategies that work for you. For example, are there any things that you do when you're feeling anxious or overwhelmed that help you calm down and feel more in control?

Also, I want to ask, have you ever had any experiences in the past where you felt like you were in a situation that was completely outside of your control, and you had to find a way to cope with it? How did you handle it, and what did you learn from the experience?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
I do have a few things that help me when I'm feeling anxious. I like to take deep breaths and count to 10 in my head. Sometimes I'll do some repetitive things like tapping my hands or walking back and forth. And if I'm really overwhelmed, I might just need to take a break and go somewhere quiet for a bit.

But, yeah, there was one time when I was in a really tough situation. I was on a trip with my family, and we got stuck in a really long traffic jam. I was feeling really anxious and overwhelmed, and my family was getting frustrated with me because I was being "too sensitive" or whatever. But, um, I don't know, I just kind of shut down, I guess. I stopped talking and just sat there, trying to calm myself down. It was pretty embarrassing, but it was the only way I could cope at the time.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you have some really helpful coping strategies that work for you, like deep breathing, counting, and repetitive movements. And it's great that you know what you need to do to calm yourself down when you're feeling overwhelmed.

I also want to acknowledge that it takes a lot of courage to share about a difficult experience like the traffic jam incident. It sounds like it was a really tough situation for you, and it's understandable that you felt anxious and overwhelmed. It's also understandable that you might have felt embarrassed or self-conscious about how you coped with it, especially if your family didn't understand what you were going through.

But I want to reassure you that it's okay to prioritize your own needs and take care of yourself, even if that means stepping back or taking a break. It's not about being "too sensitive" or anything like that - it's about recognizing what you need to feel safe and calm, and taking steps to make that happen.

I'm curious, how did you feel after the traffic jam incident? Did you talk to your family about how you were feeling, or did you just kind of move on from it? And have you noticed any patterns or triggers that might contribute to you feeling anxious or overwhelmed in situations like that?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
After the traffic jam incident...I don't know, I just kind of...shut down, like I said. I didn't really talk to my family about it, because I didn't know how to explain it. I just knew that I needed some space, and I didn't want to deal with their questions or concerns. It was pretty isolating, actually.

As for patterns or triggers, I think I'm getting a little better at recognizing them. I've been trying to pay more attention to my body and what it's telling me, when I'm feeling anxious or overwhelmed. Like, if I'm in a situation that's feeling too unpredictable or too loud, I'll start to feel this...tension, I guess. It's hard to describe, but it's like my whole body is tightening up, and I know that I need to get out of there or do something to calm down. Does that make sense?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like the traffic jam incident was a really difficult experience for you, and it's understandable that you felt like you needed to shut down and have some space. It can be really hard to explain what you're going through to others, especially if they don't understand or don't know how to support you.

I'm glad to hear that you're getting better at recognizing your patterns and triggers, though. That's a really important step in taking care of yourself and managing your anxiety. It sounds like you're developing a greater awareness of your body and what it's telling you, which can be really helpful in anticipating and preparing for situations that might be overwhelming.

The way you describe the tension in your body is really vivid, and it makes sense to me. It's like your body is sending you a signal that something is feeling off or overwhelming, and you need to take steps to calm down and regulate yourself. That's a really important thing to pay attention to, and it sounds like you're getting better at listening to your body and responding to its needs.

I want to ask, what do you think would have helped you in that traffic jam situation? If you could go back and do it again, what would you do differently? And what kind of support or understanding do you think would have made a difference for you in that moment?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
I think...I think if I could go back, I would have been more honest with my family about how I was feeling. I would have told them that I was feeling overwhelmed and anxious, and that I needed some space. But I was too scared to admit that, because I thought they would think I was being "too sensitive" or "paranoid".

And if they had been more understanding and supportive...I don't know, maybe they would have let me take a break or something. Maybe they would have acknowledged that I was feeling overwhelmed and offered to help me calm down. That would have made a big difference, I think.

But instead, they just got frustrated with me and told me to "toughen up" or "get over it". That just made me feel worse, and I ended up feeling even more isolated and alone.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you felt like you couldn't be honest with your family about how you were feeling, because you were afraid of being judged or dismissed. That must have been a really difficult and isolating experience for you.

It's understandable that you would want your family to be more understanding and supportive, especially in a moment when you were feeling overwhelmed and anxious. It's like you were crying out for help, but instead of getting the support you needed, you got criticized and told to "toughen up".

I want to acknowledge that it's not okay for someone to tell you to "get over it" or "toughen up" when you're feeling anxious or overwhelmed. That kind of response can be really hurtful and invalidating, and it's not a helpful way to support someone who is struggling.

It's great that you're recognizing what you needed in that moment, and what would have made a difference for you. That's a really important step in taking care of yourself and advocating for your own needs.

I want to ask, how do you think your family's response to your anxiety has affected your relationships with them? Do you feel like you can be open and honest with them about your feelings, or do you still feel like you need to hide or downplay your anxiety around them?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
I...I don't know, it's hard to explain. I feel like I've always been a bit wary of talking to my family about my feelings, because I'm afraid of being judged or dismissed. And now, even though I'm trying to be more honest and open with them, I still feel like I'm walking on eggshells around them.

I don't know if I can be completely open and honest with them about my anxiety, because I'm afraid of how they'll react. They've always been a bit...unsupportive, I guess, when it comes to my anxiety. They just don't get it, and they don't know how to help me.

It's like, I'm trying to be more brave and speak up, but at the same time, I'm still afraid of being rejected or dismissed. It's a really hard feeling to explain, but it's like I'm stuck between wanting to be honest and wanting to protect myself from getting hurt.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're feeling a bit trapped between wanting to be open and honest with your family, but also feeling like you need to protect yourself from their potential judgment or rejection. That's a really tough and vulnerable place to be, and I can understand why you'd feel like you're walking on eggshells around them.

It's like you're trying to navigate this delicate balance between being true to yourself and being safe, and it's not always easy to know which way to lean. On the one hand, you want to be honest and open with your family, but on the other hand, you're afraid of being hurt or rejected.

I want to acknowledge that it's okay to prioritize your own safety and well-being, especially when it comes to something as important as your mental health. It's not selfish or weak to take care of yourself and protect yourself from people who might not be supportive or understanding.

At the same time, I also want to encourage you to keep working on being brave and speaking up, even if it's scary or uncomfortable. It's possible that your family may surprise you and be more supportive than you think, or that they may learn and grow alongside you as you work on being more open and honest.

But even if that's not the case, it's still important to prioritize your own needs and take care of yourself. You deserve to be supported and understood, and it's okay to seek out people and resources that can provide that for you, even if it's not your family.

Can I ask, are there any other people in your life who you feel like you can be more open and honest with about your anxiety? Friends, maybe, or a therapist or counselor? Sometimes having a supportive community or network can make a big difference in feeling like you can be yourself and prioritize your own needs.
